newsitem.title: TAIWAN: U.S. ex-envoy's sex and bribes charges sweep Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. ex-envoy's sex and bribes charges sweep Taiwan.

text.p: Allegations by the former head of Washington's de facto embassy in Taipei that staff extorted sex and money from visa applicants swept Taiwan on Monday and one ex-employee said he had evidence to support the charges.

Officials of Taiwan's government and the American Institute in Taiwan would not comment on charges lodged on Sunday by James Wood, ex-chairman of the Washington-funded agency that handles U.S. interests in the absence of diplomatic relations.
Wood said in Washington that institute staff took bribes, that US$5.3 million in visa fees was missing and that a visa investigator forced at least one applicant to trade sex for a visa approval.

"We only learned of James Wood's allegations through the newspapers so it would be inappropriate for us to comment, especially as the case is complicated," foreign ministry spokesman Peter Cheng said.
Taiwan media gave exhaustive coverage of Wood's charges, running into detail about the alleged irregularities.
Wood said he was forced from his job when he tried to shed light on what he called widespread corruption at the institute.

"I reported the missing money, the personal profiteering and the sexual harassment to the authorities around and above me," he said. "...Instead of seeing justice served, a quiet cover-up ensued. ... I was forced to resign my position."
Institute spokeswoman Jennifer Galt declined to comment.
"We have no information about this matter and we are not going to comment on it, either," she told Reuters by telephone.
Justice Minister Liao Cheng-hao told state radio that if the victim of sexual harassment did not bring charges it would be unlikely the judiciary could do anything.
Keng Chien-chang, a former visa investigator at the American Institute's travel section, said he was willing to testify in support of Wood and had evidence to back Wood's charges.

Keng told the state-funded Central News Agency he had kept a tape recording in which a female visa applicant complained that one of Keng's former colleagues demanded sex at her home during an interview to check her qualifications for a visa.
"I am willing to go to the United States and testify for Wood. What he charged was 100 percent true," Keng told state television.
Keng said he had been dismissed for alleged profiteering after he reported the case to institute officials.
A Taipei source confirmed that the subject of the woman's allegation had been dismissed by the institute eight years ago, shortly after the complaint was filed.

Wood disputed a February 10 Los Angeles Times article that said he sought campaign contributions from Taiwanese by saying Taiwan owed U.S. President Bill Clinton money in return for his defence of the island's security interests.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Cheng said it would be "improper" for Taiwan to comment because U.S. judicial authorities had begun investigation into the campaign fund allegations.
Cheng would not say if Taiwan prosecutors would investigate the case or whether it would affect unofficial relations between the United States and Taiwan.
Taiwan has no official ties with the United States, which recognises only Taiwan's longtime arch-rival, China.
